sections.heading: What is Dynamic import() and code splitting?

blocks.text: **Dynamic import() and code splitting** is a run-time JavaScript mechanism enforced by the engine on every execution. Dynamic import() and code splitting governs how code is loaded, tree-shaken, and resolved at build time versus run time. This section defines terms before code — read the glossary, then run the snippets in Node or the browser console.

sections.heading: Why Dynamic import() and code splitting matters in production

blocks.text: Senior interviews and on-call debugging both test **Dynamic import() and code splitting** beyond one-line definitions. Production failures here look like silent data corruption, memory growth, type errors at CI, or async ordering bugs — not syntax errors. If you know C#, use the comparison table to transfer intuition instead of memorizing rules in isolation.

blocks.title: Interview trap
blocks.body: Interviewers ask "Dynamic import() and code splitting" as a follow-up to system design or debugging exercises. They want mechanism, tradeoffs, and a concrete failure you have seen — not textbook definitions.

Pitfalls for Dynamic import() and code splitting
blocks.body: Treating Dynamic import() and code splitting as pure syntax without run-time behavior. Skipping validation at API/JSON boundaries. Ignoring browser versus Node differences. Hand-waving in design review without a test or metric.

blocks.text: Prove mastery of **Dynamic import() and code splitting** with a failing test that captures the edge case, a DevTools or heap snapshot showing the bug, and a clear tradeoff statement in design review. Senior interviewers want mechanism — what the engine actually do — plus when the simple explicit version beats the clever abstraction.
